content.question_text: What is the relationship between a class and an object?

core_requirements: A class specifies how objects are made — it is the template (like a cookie cutter).
An object is a specific instance created from that class (like the cookie itself).
acceptable_variations: Class is the blueprint, object is the instance.

content.question_text: What is encapsulation, and what two things does it combine into one package?

core_requirements: Encapsulation combines data and behavior into one package.
It hides the implementation details from the users of the object, giving it 'black box' behavior.
acceptable_variations: Information hiding. Combining instance fields and methods so outside code cannot directly access internal data.

content.question_text: What is the key benefit of encapsulation's 'black box' behavior for the internal data of an object?

core_requirements: As long as the class keeps its interface (methods) consistent, it can completely change how it stores its data internally without any other object knowing or caring.
No other object can manipulate an object's data directly — only through its methods.
acceptable_variations: Internal implementation can change freely without breaking outside code.

content.question_text: What are the three key characteristics used to identify and describe any object?

core_requirements: Behavior — what methods can you apply to this object, or what can you do with it.
State — how does the object react when those methods are invoked; what does it currently look like.
Identity — how is this object distinguished from others that may have the same behavior and state.

content.question_text: What is the object's state, and can it change spontaneously on its own?

core_requirements: The state is what the object currently looks like — the information it stores about itself.
It cannot change spontaneously; any change in state must be a consequence of method calls.
acceptable_variations: State is the object's current data. It only changes via method calls, never on its own.

content.question_text: Two objects from the same class always share the same behavior and state — what still makes them distinct?

core_requirements: Their identity — each object is always a distinct object regardless of whether its state matches another.
Two orders in an order-processing system are always distinct objects even if they request identical items.
acceptable_variations: Identity is always unique per object even if state and behavior are identical.

content.question_text: When analyzing a problem description to design an OOP system, what parts of speech map to classes and methods respectively?

core_requirements: Nouns in the problem description typically map to classes.
Verbs in the problem description typically map to methods.

content.question_text: In an order-processing system, give at least three example nouns that would become classes.

core_requirements: Any three of: Item, Order, Shipping address, Payment, Account.
acceptable_variations: Any three valid nouns from the list in the book.

content.question_text: Name the three most common relationships between classes and their plain-English equivalents.

core_requirements: Dependence — 'uses-a'
Aggregation — 'has-a'
Inheritance — 'is-a'
acceptable_variations: Uses-a, Has-a, Is-a with correct relationship names.

content.question_text: What is the dependence relationship between classes, and why should you try to minimize it?

core_requirements: Dependence ('uses-a') means one class's methods use or manipulate objects of another class.
You should minimize it because if class A is unaware of class B, changes to B cannot introduce bugs into A — this reduces coupling between classes.
acceptable_variations: Fewer dependencies means changes in one class are less likely to break another.

content.question_text: What does the aggregation ('has-a') relationship mean between two classes?

core_requirements: Aggregation means objects of one class contain objects of another class.
For example, an Order object contains Item objects.
acceptable_variations: 'Has-a' means containment — one class holds instances of another.

content.question_text: What does the inheritance ('is-a') relationship express, and what does a subclass gain from it?

core_requirements: Inheritance expresses a relationship between a more specific and a more general class.
The subclass inherits methods from the superclass but also has additional capabilities of its own.
acceptable_variations: A RushOrder is-a Order — it inherits Order's methods but adds priority handling.
